documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

25 y/o woman starting a doctoral program in public health this fall; moved to Easthampton over the summer and wants a primary care home here. No complaints today.

PMH: genital HSV-2, diagnosed about three years ago by her previous PCP. Takes valacyclovir 500 mg every day for suppression and says it works; can't remember the last outbreak. Nothing else.
PSH: none.
Meds: valacyclovir 500 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: mother with hypothyroidism. Father with high blood pressure.
Social: never smoked, no alcohol, no drugs. Lives in an apartment in town. Single. Grad school full time with a research assistantship. Insurance through the university student plan.
Gyn: periods regular. Last Pap 2019 at her old office, she thinks normal. Thinks she had the HPV shots as a kid.

ROS: negative across the board.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Well-appearing. HEENT normal, neck without nodes or thyromegaly. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Skin clear. No genital exam today, no active lesions per patient.

A/P
1. Genital HSV-2, on suppression. Continue valacyclovir 500 mg daily. We'll take over refills once her current supply runs out.
2. Health maintenance. CBC, CMP, TSH (given mom's thyroid history), one-time HIV and hep C, urine chlamydia/GC. PHQ-2 is 0. Requesting old records for Pap and immunization history. Flu shot when it arrives in October.

Return for a physical next year, sooner as needed.

orders.reason: persistent diarrhea after travel to northern India

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Back 9/7 from two weeks backpacking through rural northern India. Drank untreated well water at a couple of village stops. About 5 days of loose stools 3-4 times a day that look greasy, more gas than usual, crampy lower belly pain. No fever, no vomiting, no blood. Eating less but drinking fine. Still on valacyclovir.

O: Vitals per flowsheet, afebrile. Looks well, mucous membranes moist. Abdomen soft, mildly tender diffusely, no guarding.

A/P: Post-travel diarrhea, greasy stools after untreated water, suspect a parasite such as giardia. Not dehydrated. The outside GI group runs a travel GI clinic with same-week stool microscopy, so referring there rather than sending her home with a kit; they can see her Tuesday. Hydration, bland diet. Call if fever or bleeding.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Referral
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Referral to gastroenterology, travel GI clinic. 27 y/o woman with about 5 days of greasy diarrhea, flatulence and cramps after drinking untreated well water during travel in rural northern India. Afebrile, no blood. History of genital HSV-2 on valacyclovir 500 mg daily. NKDA. Please evaluate for parasitic infection. Appointment 9/19.

medications.sig: Take 4 tablets (2 g) by mouth once with food

results.text: Occasional Giardia cysts seen. Fat droplets present.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY CONSULTATION, travel GI clinic
Date of visit: 09/19/2023
Referred by: primary care

Reason: diarrhea after travel.

History: 27-year-old graduate student, back about two weeks from a two-week backpacking trip in rural northern India during which she drank untreated well water. For 10 days she has had loose, greasy stools, increased flatulence and crampy abdominal pain. She denies fever, nausea and vomiting. LMP about two weeks ago. Sexually active with a male partner and does not always use condoms.

PMH: genital HSV-2 on suppression. PSH: none.
Medications: valacyclovir 500 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: hypothyroidism in her mother, hypertension in her father.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, graduate student in public health.

Exam: T 36.9 C, BP 112/70, P 78, RR 16. Well-appearing. Abdomen mildly distended with hyperactive bowel sounds; diffusely tender to deep palpation, without rebound or guarding. No hepatosplenomegaly.

Studies today: stool microscopy shows fat droplets and occasional cysts consistent with Giardia. Urine pregnancy test negative.

Impression: giardiasis acquired from untreated water during travel.

Plan: tinidazole 2 g by mouth as a single dose with food, given in clinic today. Avoid alcohol for 72 hours (she does not drink). Hydration. Hand hygiene and household precautions reviewed. Lactose may be poorly tolerated for a few weeks. No routine test of cure if symptoms resolve; call us if not better in 1 to 2 weeks.

Thank you for this referral.
Gastroenterology

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Arrival 06/10/2024 13:40

CC: yellow eyes, exhausted, nauseated.

HPI: 28-year-old woman with genital HSV-2 on daily valacyclovir and giardiasis treated in September 2023. Several days of steadily worsening fatigue, then yellowing of her skin and eyes, upper abdominal discomfort, nausea and urine the color of tea. She returned on 5/24 from a roughly ten-week public health field placement in a rural area with limited clean water, where the community had an outbreak of diarrheal illness while she was there. Never transfused. Has not taken acetaminophen. Does not drink. No tattoos, no injection drug use.

Meds: valacyclovir 500 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: mother hypothyroid, father hypertensive.

Exam: BP 94/58, HR 114, RR 18, T 37.4, SpO2 97% RA. Lethargic but rouses to voice and answers appropriately. Deeply jaundiced with scleral icterus. Liver edge palpable well below the costal margin, tender. Mild shifting dullness. Lungs clear. Heart tachycardic, regular. No rash.

ED course: IV fluid bolus, then maintenance fluids, with heart rate improving. Labs: ALT 2,860, AST 2,210, alk phos 196, T bili 8.4 (direct 6.1), albumin 3.2, PT 22.1, INR 2.0. CBC and BMP unremarkable. Acute hepatitis serologies sent; hepatitis E IgM returned positive this evening.

Impression: acute hepatitis E with coagulopathy and lethargy, likely acquired during field placement.
Disposition: admitted to medicine, hepatology consulting.

reports.text: RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT ULTRASOUND WITH DOPPLER. Indication: acute hepatitis, coagulopathy. Liver enlarged, 18.5 cm in craniocaudal length, with homogeneous echotexture and no focal lesion. Gallbladder normal, no stones. Common bile duct normal in caliber; no intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilation. Small amount of perihepatic free fluid. Main portal vein patent with normal hepatopetal flow; hepatic veins patent. Spleen normal in size. Right kidney normal.
reports.conclusion: Hepatomegaly with small-volume perihepatic ascites. No biliary dilation or focal liver lesion. Patent portal and hepatic veins.

documents.title: Hepatology Consultation
documents.author: hepatology
documents.body:
HEPATOLOGY INPATIENT CONSULTATION, 06/11/2024

Asked to see a 28-year-old with acute hepatitis and INR 2.0 on arrival. Previously healthy liver; normal liver tests at her primary care office in 2021 and 2023. Returned late May from ten weeks of fieldwork in a rural area with poor water access and a diarrheal outbreak. Anti-HEV IgM positive; hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, HBc IgM and HCV antibody negative; not pregnant. Ultrasound: enlarged liver, small perihepatic ascites, patent vessels, no biliary dilation.

This morning INR 2.3, T bili 9.1, ALT 2,410. Drowsy but oriented, follows commands.

Assessment: acute hepatitis E with acute liver injury and coagulopathy. Valacyclovir is not a concern at this dose and can continue.

Recommendations: supportive care, avoid sedatives and hepatotoxic drugs, daily hepatic panel and INR, glucose checks, close mental status watch. No antiviral therapy indicated. We will follow.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 06/10/2024, discharged 06/15/2024
Principal diagnosis: acute hepatitis E with coagulopathy.

Course: Admitted from the ED with jaundice, lethargy, mild ascites and INR 2.0. IV fluids; blood pressure and heart rate normalized within the first day. Hepatology followed. INR peaked at 2.3 on 6/11 and mentation was back to baseline by 6/12. Labs improved daily: 6/13 ALT 1,520, AST 980, T bili 7.2, INR 1.7. On 6/15 ALT 910, AST 520, alk phos 172, T bili 5.2 (direct 3.8), albumin 3.2, PT 16.3, INR 1.4. Tolerating a regular diet, walking the halls. No transfusion, no procedures.

Other workup: hepatitis A, B and C negative; urine hCG negative. RUQ ultrasound with Doppler: hepatomegaly, small perihepatic ascites, patent vessels.

Discharge medications: valacyclovir 500 mg daily (unchanged). No acetaminophen for now; no alcohol.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within one week with hepatic panel and INR; hepatology clinic as needed if labs stall. Return for confusion, bleeding, worsening jaundice or abdominal swelling.

documents.title: Admission Notification
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Admission notice received: patient admitted last night through the regional hospital ED with acute hepatitis. Spoke with her mother, who is listed as emergency contact and called the office; patient awake and talking this morning. Flagged for PCP. Will book a post-discharge visit once we have a discharge date.

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
HOSPITAL FOLLOW-UP

Admitted 6/10 to 6/15 at the regional hospital with acute hepatitis E, acquired on her spring field placement; INR went as high as 2.3 and she was drowsy the first day. ED record, hepatology consult and discharge summary reviewed.

Since home: energy maybe half of normal, napping in the afternoons. Appetite returning, no vomiting. Urine lighter. No confusion, no bleeding or bruising, belly not swollen. No acetaminophen, no alcohol. Taking valacyclovir.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet, normal. Tired-appearing but alert and quick. Sclerae still icteric, skin faintly yellow. Abdomen soft, liver edge just palpable and nontender, no shifting dullness. No asterixis. No bruising.

A/P
Acute hepatitis E, recovering. Repeat today; will message results. If the trend continues, liver tests again in 3 weeks. Rest, hydrate, advance activity as tolerated. Hand hygiene at home. Avoid acetaminophen and alcohol until labs normalize. She asked about returning to her research job: remote work fine now. Return or call for confusion, bleeding, or worsening jaundice.

documents.title: Liver Test Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your liver numbers from Wednesday are much better than at discharge: ALT down to 480 from 910, bilirubin 3.6 from 5.2, and your clotting test (INR) is 1.2, nearly normal. Exactly the direction we want. Let's recheck around July 10; the front desk will reach out to schedule a lab visit.

documents.title: Liver Test Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Big improvement: ALT 96, bilirubin 1.4, INR 1.1. Almost back to normal. One more check in about six weeks, late August. How is your energy?

documents.title: Re: Liver Test Results
documents.author: patient
documents.body: So much better! Back to working most of the day, and my eyes aren't yellow anymore. I'll book the August lab.

documents.title: Result Note
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hepatic panel and INR normal. Acute hepatitis E has resolved; no further liver testing needed. Problem resolved. Portal note sent.

documents.title: Liver Tests Normal
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: All of your liver tests are normal now. The hepatitis E is behind you, and nothing more to check. Fine to use acetaminophen again at normal doses. Good luck with the semester.

documents.author: obstetrics

Dear colleague,

We saw your patient for her first prenatal visit on 11/12/2024. She is a 29-year-old G1P0 at 9 weeks 3 days by LMP. Transvaginal dating ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity; crown-rump length agrees with her dates, and we are keeping the EDD of 6/14/2025.

History reviewed: genital HSV-2 on valacyclovir 500 mg daily, which she will continue; hepatitis E in June 2024, resolved; giardiasis in 2023, treated. No surgeries. NKDA.

Prenatal labs drawn at this visit were unremarkable, and she is rubella immune. Pap is current from 2022.

Plan: routine prenatal visits, anatomy scan at 20 weeks, glucose screening at 24 to 28 weeks. We discussed HSV in pregnancy and that any prodrome or lesion near term needs an urgent call, since active lesions in labor mean cesarean delivery. Prenatal vitamin daily.

Thank you for the referral.
Obstetrics

documents.title: Operative Note: Cesarean Delivery
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OPERATIVE NOTE
Date: 06/11/2025

Preoperative diagnosis: intrauterine pregnancy at 39 weeks 4 days in active labor; active genital herpes lesions.
Postoperative diagnosis: same; delivered.
Procedure: emergent primary low transverse cesarean delivery.
Anesthesia: spinal.

Indication: 29-year-old G1 with genital HSV-2 on daily valacyclovir suppression, admitted in active labor with regular contractions and cervical change. She had no fever, urinary burning or abnormal discharge. On exam there were several clustered vesicles on a red base over the labia and perineum. With active lesions in labor, vaginal birth would expose the baby to HSV, so we proceeded with cesarean.

Findings: viable male infant from vertex position, Apgars 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. Normal uterus, tubes and ovaries. Clear fluid.

Uncomplicated procedure. Pfannenstiel skin incision closed subcuticularly. Mother and infant to recovery in stable condition.

documents.title: Obstetric Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRIC DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 06/11/2025, discharged 06/14/2025

Diagnoses: term pregnancy, delivered by emergent primary low transverse cesarean for active genital HSV lesions in labor. Genital HSV-2 on suppression. Past history of acute hepatitis E (2024, resolved) and giardiasis (2023, treated).

Course: delivered a healthy boy on 6/11 (Apgars 8 and 9). No rash, breathing trouble or enlarged liver or spleen on newborn exam; pediatrics is following him for the HSV exposure per protocol. Her recovery was routine: afebrile, incision clean, pain controlled with oral medicines, ambulating, voiding, tolerating a diet. Valacyclovir continued throughout.

Discharge medications:
- valacyclovir 500 mg by mouth daily
- prenatal vitamin daily
- ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as needed, about 2 weeks
- acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 6 hours as needed, about 2 weeks
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: incision check at 2 weeks, postpartum visit at 6 weeks. Call for fever, heavy bleeding, incision redness or drainage, or low mood.

documents.title: Postpartum Check-in Call

documents.body: Called after receiving delivery records. Home since Saturday with her son. Incision sore but improving, using ibuprofen a few times a day. No fever, bleeding tapering. Baby feeding and seen by pediatrics yesterday, she says he is doing fine. Sleep is in pieces but mood okay, has help at home. OB incision check next week. Reminded to keep taking valacyclovir and to call with any concerns.

Recovering well. Incision healed. Bleeding has stopped. Postpartum depression screen negative. Pelvic exam normal, no lesions. Cleared for exercise and usual activity. Continuing valacyclovir 500 mg daily. Cervical screening due this fall with primary care.

We will see her as needed. Thank you.
Obstetrics

events.reason: Confusion, headache, found beside gas heater

reports.text: Sinus tachycardia, rate 110. Normal axis and intervals. No ST elevation or depression, no T-wave inversion.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Arrival 06/08/2026 18:25 by EMS

CC: confusion.

HPI: 30-year-old woman with genital HSV-2 on valacyclovir, whose last outbreak was at delivery in 2025 and led to a cesarean. Per her roommate, she had a headache, felt dizzy and nauseated from the morning on and said she would sleep it off. Later the roommate found her drowsy and muddled on the couch beside an unvented gas space heater that had been running in the apartment. Roommate reports no drugs or alcohol and no fall or injury.

PMH: genital HSV-2; giardiasis 2023, treated; acute hepatitis E 2024, resolved. PSH: cesarean 2025.
Meds: valacyclovir 500 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: P 110, RR 20, BP 122/70, T 37.1. Confused, speech mildly slurred. Skin flushed bright red. Lungs clear. Heart tachycardic, regular, no murmur. Clumsy rapid alternating movements bilaterally; strength full and symmetric, no focal deficit.

Course: 100% oxygen by nonrebreather started on arrival. Pulse oximeter then read 96%, which is not reassuring here: a standard probe reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin. Arterial blood gas with co-oximetry: carboxyhemoglobin 26%, pH 7.36, PaCO2 35, PaO2 412 on nonrebreather, bicarbonate 20. Lactate 2.6. hs-troponin I 4. Urine hCG negative. CBC normal; BMP normal except bicarbonate 21. Monitor and 12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ischemic changes.

Impression: carbon monoxide poisoning from an unvented gas heater, with confusion and cerebellar signs; airway intact.
Disposition: discussed with hyperbaric medicine; transferred on 100% oxygen to the regional hyperbaric unit. Fire department notified to check the apartment.

documents.title: Hyperbaric Medicine Discharge Summary
documents.author: hyperbaric medicine
documents.body:
HYPERBARIC MEDICINE DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 06/08/2026, discharged 06/09/2026

Diagnosis: acute carbon monoxide poisoning (carboxyhemoglobin 26% at the sending ED) with confusion, slurred speech and impaired rapid alternating movements.

Course: arrived on 100% oxygen. Three hyperbaric oxygen sessions within 24 hours, the first started on arrival. Carboxyhemoglobin 2% after the first session. Tolerated all sessions; ears equalized without difficulty. By the next morning she was fully oriented, speech normal, rapid alternating movements normal, gait steady. No chest pain.

Discharge: home 06/09. Valacyclovir 500 mg daily, unchanged. NKDA.
Instructions: no gas heater use until the appliance is inspected or removed; working CO detectors on every level. Delayed neurologic symptoms can appear in the weeks after CO poisoning; call for trouble with memory, concentration, mood, movement or new headaches. PCP follow-up within one week.
